title: Sales Engineer — Race Track Compliance Systems
description:
What we are building


**We are hiring a field team, in the hundreds.**
------------------------------------------------


Rural agriculture is short of people, and we have said so on our company page. It would be a hollow thing to argue that and then run this company from an office. Over the coming years we intend to hire hundreds into the field — people who work in the districts where the animals are, alongside the farmers and dairy staff who care for them.


*01***Field\-deployed data scientists**
Not data scientists who visit a farm. Data scientists based near the herds, who calibrate models against the animals in front of them, and who will know within a week when a model is wrong because they will be standing next to the reason.


*02***Agriculture interns**
Agriculture and veterinary graduates who want their first year of work to be spent in sheds and yards rather than in a training room. We would rather teach data science to someone who understands cattle than the reverse.


*03***Field technicians**
Fitting, servicing and commissioning sensors and gateways, and training the caretakers who use them. Hired in the district, trained by us, working with the same farms year after year.


What we screen for, before any qualification


* You like the people who do this work. Farmers, dairy staff, goshala caretakers, stockmen — not as beneficiaries of your expertise, but as the ones who know things you do not.
* You will go to the animal. The best model in this company was improved by somebody who noticed something in a shed, not in a notebook.
* You can explain it so a farmer understands it. If a recommendation does not land in plain words, in her language, it has not landed.
* You will say when the data is wrong. We would rather hear it from you than from a veterinarian, and far rather than from a trustee.
Hiring at this scale happens district by district and follows deployments, not the other way round. We do not open a role in a place we are not working, and we do not fly people in to a district where somebody local could do the job better.


If you are reading this and none of the roles listed below is yours, write anyway. Tell us the district you know and what you have done in it.


  
How to apply


Send your resume and a short cover letter to **hr@hanuinnotech.com** or **svuppalapati@hanuinnotech.com**, with the role title in the subject line.
  
Before the résumé


We hire people who are willing to stand in a shed in the rain and then go home and improve a model.*Both halves matter. A model built by someone who has never stood in the rain gets the wrong things right. A day in the rain that does not change the model helps one farm once.*


**What we ask of everyone**
---------------------------


Sales Engineers, Field Engineers, Data Interns and Business Development Account Executives — whatever the title, the same things are non\-negotiable.


01
#### **Love to see farmers succeed**


Not tolerate it. Not serve it as a market. Actually want it, and be visibly pleased when a herd comes through a bad season because somebody acted on an alert. If a farmer's win does not feel like your win, this is the wrong company.


02
#### **Understand the farmer and their pain points**


Sit with them. Learn what the season costs, what the loan repayment falls due against, why the last technology they were sold is in a drawer. You cannot solve a problem you have only read about, and nobody here gets to design for a farm they have never stood on.


03
#### **Explain it so a farmer understands it**


Every recommendation must land in plain words, in their own language, in the time they have between milkings. If it needs a slide deck to make sense, it is not finished. Clarity is not a courtesy here — it is the product working.


04
#### **Own the problem to the outcome**


Passion to own the problem end to end, and to make sure the customer actually succeeds — with benefits you can point at, for farmers, banks, insurance providers and every customer we serve. Not a handover. Not a ticket closed. The result.


05
#### **Feel what a four\-legged customer cannot say**


We need people who feel the pain of our four\-legged customers, and who serve the humans who dearly love them. Animals must be treated humanely, and you play an important role in that — a role we reward.


06
#### **Persistent, and willing to think outside the box**


Rural deployment does not go to plan. Networks fail, seasons turn, the obvious answer is often the wrong one. We need people who stay with a problem after it becomes inconvenient, and who look for the answer nobody in the room has suggested yet.


How this shows up in what you are paid


If farmers' revenue increases, you are paid a bonus. If animals are treated humanely and you played a part in it, you are rewarded. We tie reward to the outcomes we say we care about, because a mission that costs nothing to ignore is not a mission.


You are working for more than a pay


Every person here is working towards something larger than the salary: real difference in the world, and a future in which the next generation has opportunity where they already live.


A young person in Anand or Srinagar or Vizianagaram should not have to leave for a city to find work worth doing. If the analytics that make a herd profitable are built where the herd is, the work stays there too. Localised opportunity is not a by\-product of this business — it is the point of it.


And what is built locally travels. The models trained on a Kashmir winter serve temperate Europe and Central Asia. The mango forecasts built for Philippine smallholders serve a global bottler. Local opportunity and global prosperity are the same project, run in the right order.


We hire for this before we hire for the résumé. The technical skill can be taught; this cannot.


  
Equine roles


### **For the horse sensor roles specifically**


Sales Engineers and Account Executives promoting the Hayagriva HG Model 3 must be able to hold a credible conversation with four very different rooms, often in the same week.


**Race club owners**
Commercial owners of racing clubs and yards, who will ask what the sensor protects and what it costs against the value of the animal.


**Government agencies**
Procurement, welfare and compliance officers buying at institutional scale, with the process and documentation that requires.


**Police and military units**
Mounted police and military or ceremonial establishments, where the animal is operational and readiness is the requirement.


**Professional race trainers**
The people closest to the horse, who will judge the product on whether it tells them something they did not already know.


The finding these roles rest on


Tracks that publish their injury data record roughly a third fewer fatalities than tracks that do not — 0\.88 against 1\.27 per 1,000 starts. The act of measuring, in public, is associated with the animals coming home. That is the whole argument for a sensor on a horse: not that any single injury was preventable, but that a yard which watches continuously sees more than a yard which watches at exercise.


If you cannot say that sentence to a steward and mean every word of it, these are not your roles.


  
The person who makes it work on the ground. You install HG sensors across a club's stabled population, prove the data holds through a racing season, and turn it into a compliance record the club's stewards will accept.


Responsibilities


* Design and deliver HG Sensor deployments across a club's yards, from pilot to full population
* Install, commission and service sensors, and run the calibration that teaches the models each animal
* Build the injury and welfare reporting a club needs for its stewards, its regulator and — where it chooses — publication
* Specify HG Sensor Core or HG Sensor Enterprise on\-site hosting where a club cannot or will not connect to an outside network
* Train club staff, trainers, grooms and veterinary teams on what the alerts mean and what to do about them
* Sit at the track on race days and see whether the system earned its place
What we look for


* Engineering or data science background, with hands\-on comfort — you will be fitting hardware, not presenting slides about it
* Able to explain a model's output to a trainer in the words a trainer uses
* Comfortable around horses and trained, or willing to be trained, in safe handling
* Willing to travel across Indian race centres and work to a racing calendar rather than an office one
* Understands that a claim you cannot support costs more than a sale you did not make
